If you're planning to hire in Zambia, the question isn't whether compliance matters. It's whether you want to manage it yourself or hand it off. Registering your own entity means owning NAPSA, NHIMA, PAYE, and every update that follows. An EOR takes that off your plate from day one, and for most companies at early headcount in Zambia, the math strongly favors it.


**TLDR:**


- An EOR lets you hire in Zambia without a local entity, handling NAPSA, NHIMA, PAYE, and Employment Code Act 2019 compliance for you
- Zambia requires 24 days annual leave, 14 weeks paid maternity leave, and tiered termination notice up to 30 days, costs many foreign employers miss
- EOR runs around 70% less in total cost compared to maintaining your own Zambian entity, where fixed overhead applies regardless of headcount
- A local Zambian entity makes more sense at large, permanent headcount or when equity administration requires direct employer control
- Bolto's EOR service covers Zambia with employees onboarded in as little as 48 hours, no Zambian entity required


## What Is an Employer of Record in Zambia


An Employer of Record (EOR) is a third-party company that becomes the legal employer on paper while you stay in control of the day-to-day work. In Zambia, that means the EOR holds the employment contract, handles registration under the Employment Code Act 2019, manages NAPSA (National Pension Scheme Authority) contributions, and meets NHIMA (National Health Insurance Management Authority) obligations. You direct what the employee does. The EOR handles everything the Zambian government requires of a local employer.


This matters because Zambia is a commercially active market. Commercial activity spans mining, energy, agriculture, infrastructure, manufacturing, and ICT, and companies hiring there need employment structure, payroll, and statutory registrations sorted before anyone starts work. For broader context, see this[EOR international hiring and expansion guide](https://www.bolto.com/blog/eor-international-global-hiring-expansion-guide) .


## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in Zambia


Zambia's employment framework is more detailed than many foreign employers expect. The Employment Code Act 2019 (Act 3 of 2019) consolidates the country's labor standards and governs every employment relationship, from contracts to termination. It is the primary compliance reference for any foreign company hiring there.


Under Zambia's Employment Code Act 2019 and tax framework, employers are generally required to register with tax authorities, run payroll under Pay As You Earn (PAYE) rules, and meet mandatory social contribution schemes. These obligations apply before an employee's first day. Understanding what[employer of record services include](https://www.bolto.com/blog/employer-of-record-services-how-to-choose) can help you assess what to look for.


### Social Contributions: NAPSA and NHIMA


Two schemes apply to all employees.[National Pension Scheme Authority (NAPSA) contributions](https://remotepeople.com/countries/zambia/employer-of-record/) run at roughly 5% from both employer and employee (NAPSA, 2026). National Health Insurance Management Authority (NHIMA) contributions are generally 1% each (NHIMA, 2026). Both schemes generally require employer registration and regular remittance.

### Leave, Probation, Termination, and Working Hours


- Statutory annual leave is a minimum of 24 days per year, and standard working hours run to 48 per week.
- Under the Employment Code Act 2019, probation periods generally extend up to 3 months, though parties may agree to a longer period.
- Maternity leave is 14 weeks, fully paid, a material cost line many foreign employers miss in initial budgets.
- [Termination](https://globalpeoplestrategist.com/zambia/) under the Employment Code Act 2019 follows a tiered notice structure: 24 hours for contracts under one month, 14 days for one to three months, and 30 days beyond three months. Under that Act, any contract over six months generally requires written notice, and notice generally cannot be served while an employee is on leave.
- Gratuity obligations for longer-tenure employees add further exit costs that tend to surprise direct-hire budgets.

## EOR vs. Local Entity in Zambia: Which Is Right for You


When EOR works best for most companies entering Zambia, the reasons tend to cluster around a few common situations:


- You are making your first hire or a small number of hires, and fixed entity overhead would outweigh the savings.
- The[Employment Code Act 2019](https://zambialii.org/akn/zm/act/2019/3/eng@2019-04-12) and its NAPSA, NHIMA, and PAYE obligations are unfamiliar territory.
- Speed matters and you cannot wait weeks or months for entity registration to clear.
- Your long-term headcount commitment in Zambia is uncertain, and you want an exit path that does not require entity dissolution proceedings.


At a certain scale and time horizon, the math changes.
